MOVING THE MASSES WITH ELECTRICITY [6174]

By: Marion Edmunds | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight we meet the mobility masterminds plugging South Africa into an electric mass transport future

Unique Selling Point:
We have exclusive access to three innovative projects which test the future options for the mass transport sector – each with a different story, engineering mastermind and different type of vehicle
Visually appealing as we will have access to the depots and work rooms, and a factory where electric vehicles are made locally
Interesting as we have access to the information emerging from pilots projects which flags the challenges of introducing electricity to this mass public sector, including the danger of unregulated charging of vehicles pushing over the grid

Summary:
We explore three two case studies and a pilot project which are starting to shape the way electric vehicles will impact on the public transport sector – commuter buses, taxis and delivery of freight.

South Africa is lagging dangerously behind many countries in the world in the shift to to electric transport and faces many challenges, not least the difficulty of charging a new fleets of vehicles while our electricity grid is so unsteady. We have about 1000 EV’s on the road – there are 6,5 million on roads across the globe.

Cape Town’s oldest bus company and newest electric vehicle manufacturer are throwing up some answers to how to tackle this pending energy revolution, while a pilot project involving an engineering consortium, local students and taxi drivers in Stellenbosch is hoping to explore best practice solutions to herald a shift in the taxi industry. Ultimately this would see about 400 000 vehicles powered by fossil fuels replaced by electric-charged vehicles, dependent on a new charging infrastructure,in an industry that is highly competitive but notoriously unregulated.


Further information:
The first case study, Golden Arrow, is the largest and oldest bus company in Cape Town, transporting 220-thousand commuters daily on diesel-fuelled buses. Their lead electrical engineer Gideon Neethling has been conducting a year long experiment with two electric buses to build a business case for going completely electric, and lesson the company’s huge carbon footprint. However, it is only feasible he says, if South Africa starts its own bus-building industry because importing the buses undermines the commercial feasibility due to sky-high import tariffs. And it requires the buses to feed principally off Eskom power, with solar as a green accessory rather than a sole provider of energy.

The second case study is a company that wanted to enter the taxi industry, by building three-wheel electric vehicles that could carry two paying passengers at a time. Mellowcabs claims to be the first electric vehicle manufacturer in South Africa. It was founded by an environmentalist and innovator, Neil du Preez, as a start up in 2014, but once set up, he found the complexity of South African taxi transport too daunting. So he modified the taxi to a van, and shifted the company’s focus to last mile freight delivery as that industry boomed in lockdown. As a company, it’s a good South African news story employing local graduates, using local parts and gearing up in its small Stellenbosch factory to expand as orders start coming in.

The third case study holds the most potential to change the way the sector runs, but is probably the most fraught. A consortium of academics and transport engineers are importing an electric minibus taxi to run a pilot project on it in Stellenbosch, using students from the university collaborating with the local taxi industry. This project is to test how easy it will be to adapt an electric taxi to a uniquely African environment, taking into account the effect of how taxis are driven by local drivers, and the need for speedy recharging between taxi runs. This study will feed into the decision-making process required to shift South Africa’s estimated 400-thousand minibus taxis into a greener future.

Press Release:


Electric Avenue
With fossil fuel prices soaring and climate change concerns peaking, now would seem like a good time to start the electric vehicle revolution. But with only a few thousand private electric vehicles on South African roads, will it be up to mass transport projects to bring the country in line with new technology, and global mobility trends? Less than a quarter of the nation’s households own a car, so the real challenge is how to shift minibus taxis and passenger buses from diesel and petrol to electric, on cash-strapped budgets, to reduce the clunky carbon footprint of the transport industry. Carte Blanche meets the innovative engineers behind early projects that will shape the roll out of electric vehicles to move the masses – despite the crisis of loadshedding.
Producer: Marion Edmunds | Presenter: Claire Mawisa


Script:


(VO)
It’s 5am at the Golden Arrow bus depot near the airport in Cape Town.
Every weekday, more than 200-thousand people board these buses.
All diesel-powered, burning 25 million litres of fuel a year.


(VO)
But this morning, these commuters are boarding an electric bus, as part of an investigation into how to shift this company to cheaper, cleaner electric power.

Claire Mawisa Piece to Camera
This is one of only two electric buses operating on South African roads.
And its journey here in the Cape over the last year has been so successful,
that it heralds a new era for the Golden Arrow Bus Company as it signals a move away from dirty diesel.

(VO) Gideon Neethling is the engineer driving the company’s electric future.


Gideon Neethling: The test results have been really positive, we found that that the buses are really energy efficient, they're reliable. They meet all the safety requirements that we said, and the passengers and the drivers are really positive about the result.

Claire: So where in that journey are you eventually saving money?

Gideon Neethling: The bulk of the savings will come from energy. If you look at diesel, we we estimate that we probably going to see a 70% reduction in our energy cost.

Gideon Neethling: In other parts of the world, people are being sponsored to go green. That's not the case in South Africa. So we have to make sure that it's commercial solution first, with serious fringe benefit of carbon reduction.


(VO)
The two buses are charged in-house – if the electric fleet grows, so will the demand for power at peak times. But Gideon already has a plan - solar panels on the roofs of the bus depots. They want to expand to cover 22 hectares.

(VO)
Golden Arrow will still rely on Eskom to start with, but it’s a big step towards cleaner power.

Gideon Neethling: If we look at this graph, then where you see red we are using the electricity that we buying from the City of Cape Town. Where you see blue. It's where we're using our own generated electricity. So that's all renewables. And where you see green, it's where we actually export electricity to the City of Cape Town. We are putting electricity back into the grid.

Claire Mawisa Piece to Camera
The Golden Arrow Bus Service is a big hitter in Cape Town’s transport industry with its massive fleet and 3000 staff - it has the muscle to tackle the energy transition head on. …
But a short distance away in Stellenbosch is a much smaller start-up company with only 25 employees – relying on innovative engineering to move into the market.

(VO) This is a Mellowvan – a nippy three-wheel electric delivery van with a big story behind it, already on roads around South Africa.

Neil du Preez: Firstly, this is the electric motor. It's a brand new fifth generation electric motor, very light, very powerful. It climbs like a mountain goat. And obviously it's super dependable that basically never breaks.

(VO)Founder Neil du Preez tells us the charger plugs into a normal 220 volt wall socket - the battery powers the vehicle for around 120 kilometres, on a single charge. The Mellowvan is testament to local innovation.

Neil du Preez: Initially, we were faced with, we were trying to build something that we couldn't find any components for on the open market. So we had to design quite a few of the components including the battery management system, the charging system, and from there on, we kind of evolved.

(VO)
Neil’s original plan was to build a small electric two-person passenger cab….…..but delivery vans have proved more profitable……..Which begs the question, how easy will it be for the taxi industry to participate in the pending electric transport revolution?

Claire Mawisa Piece to Camera
The minibus sector shoulders by far the biggest transport burden in the country with about 350-thousand vehicles on the road. As the world shifts to electric vehicles, a consortium of engineers and academics are trying to figure out how to electrify this unique and at times unpredictable sector.

(VO) Professor Thinus Booysen from the University of Stellenbosch is part of a team working on this puzzle.

Thinus talking to taxi owners: In the rest of the world all the vehicles are transforming to electric vehicles. …CUT… So owners like you are going to have to start thinking about where do we get the vehicles? And think about how do these vehicles work? How do you fill them up? Where do you charge them? How long does it take to charge?

The researchers are importing an electric taxi to conduct experiments.

Professor Thinus Booysen
Chair of the Internet of Things, University of Stellenbosch:
Electric vehicles are viable for the public sector, but it's very important how we do it. And when we do it. There are many constraints that you need to take into account. If we just bring in electric vehicles right now, it's going to be devastating for our grid, our electrical grid with Eskom in the state that it is, can't even supply our electricity needs as it is. So with every instance of an electric vehicle being added to it, charging from it, we're increasing this load and putting extra burden on the grid.

(VO)
Students are already involved in mass surveys of the daily routes and rhythms of local taxis associations, feeding data into a complex study.

Thinus: It’s called a heatmap, so the more often they are in a space, the more dark red the colour is.
Claire: Are those ranks, are those CBD’s?
Thinus: That’s everywhere the taxi went.

Professor Thinus Booysen
Chair of the Internet of Things, University of Stellenbosch
We've taken students, put them in taxis and driven all around Stellenbosch and measured per second what the mobility patterns of these vehicles look like, so that we can extract using pure physics, how much energy needs to come from the battery in order to do so.

(VO)It’s early days in the consultation with taxi owners – but already here in Kayamandi, outside Stellenbosch, there are more questions than answers.

Zolile Mnyanda,
Kyamandi Taxi Association
Probably the battery is gonna be the most expensive, the battery … it’s our worry is going to be on the battery, how much is going to be? Another question that I thought I was supposed to ask him which company did you make those, because usually having a Toyotas and Nissans, which one is that for the battery, which makes that?

(VO) The make and origin of electric taxis is a hot topic. South Africa slaps high tariffs on imported electric vehicles, making them expensive to buy, despite being cheaper to run.

Prof Thinus Booysen
The taxi owners, they are business people, then they know how to run a business, and they care about money, making money. I think as soon as the penny drops, that there's a business opportunity here, then they will be invested, they will care enough to transition much quicker. For me the big stumbling block at the moment is the manufacturing, we need to manufacture electric vehicles locally, and specifically taxi.

(VO) Mellowvans has shown how local engineers have got the manufacture of electric vehicles right, with designs fit for purpose, extending to vehicle tracking.

Neil: We can even look down into the battery on a cell level, look at the temperature, the voltage, and that really is important to really guarantee a really long life for the vehicle.

(VO) Back at Golden Arrow, there are scores of technicians who know their way around an internal combustion engine with their eyes closed. The shift to electric will change their world, as much as the bus and taxi owners, drivers and commuters on the street.

July 4 T217 Gideon: 17:54 There is no building of electric buses in South Africa at the moment. So importing is probably the easiest way to go. We think that that's the wrong way to go, that we need to manufacture them in South Africa, that we can protect the local market, and that we can create the jobs that are required.

PROMOS:

PROMO 1:

Cape Town’s biggest bus company is running the first electric buses on South African roads.

Gideon Neethling: The bulk of the savings will come from energy. If you look at diesel, we we estimate that we are probably going to see a 70% reduction in our energy cost.

As the loadshedding crisis deepens, and fuel prices soar, it’s a much-watched move from dirty diesel to cleaner, cheaper energy.

PROMO 2:
Transporting people and goods with battery power - tonight we meet innovators who are gearing up for the electric revolution.

Neil du Preez: It's a brand new fifth generation electric motor, very light, very powerful. It climbs like a mountain goat. And obviously it's super dependable that basically never breaks.

ELEVEN SECOND PROMO:

Moving the masses with electricity - a new era of battery powered vehicles is dawning in South Africa.

Ultimately this would see about 400 000 vehicles powered by fossil fuels replaced by electric-charged vehicles, dependent on a new charging infrastructure,in an industry that is highly competitive but notoriously unregulated.
metadata.Further information: The first case study, Golden Arrow, is the largest and oldest bus company in Cape Town, transporting 220-thousand commuters daily on diesel-fuelled buses. Their lead electrical engineer Gideon Neethling has been conducting a year long experiment with two electric buses to build a business case for going completely electric, and lesson the company’s huge carbon footprint. However, it is only feasible he says, if South Africa starts its own bus-building industry because importing the buses undermines the commercial feasibility due to sky-high import tariffs. And it requires the buses to feed principally off Eskom power, with solar as a green accessory rather than a sole provider of energy. The second case study is a company that wanted to enter the taxi industry, by building three-wheel electric vehicles that could carry two paying passengers at a time. Mellowcabs claims to be the first electric vehicle manufacturer in South Africa. It was founded by an environmentalist and innovator, Neil du Preez, as a start up in 2014, but once set up, he found the complexity of South African taxi transport too daunting. So he modified the taxi to a van, and shifted the company’s focus to last mile freight delivery as that industry boomed in lockdown. As a company, it’s a good South African news story employing local graduates, using local parts and gearing up in its small Stellenbosch factory to expand as orders start coming in. The third case study holds the most potential to change the way the sector runs, but is probably the most fraught. A consortium of academics and transport engineers are importing an electric minibus taxi to run a pilot project on it in Stellenbosch, using students from the university collaborating with the local taxi industry. This project is to test how easy it will be to adapt an electric taxi to a uniquely African environment, taking into account the effect of how taxis are driven by local drivers, and the need for speedy recharging between taxi runs. This study will feed into the decision-making process required to shift South Africa’s estimated 400-thousand minibus taxis into a greener future.
